How Going Public Works and What It Means for Investors What Is an IPO? How Going Public Works and What It Means for Investors By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated November 25, 2026 · How we review An IPO, or initial public offering, happens when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time and lists on a stock exchange. Going public raises cash and creates a tradable stock, but it also brings added costs, disclosure requirements, and outside pressure that a private company never faces. This guide explains how a company actually goes public, the real benefits and downsides, and the details most overviews skip: lockup expirations, why retail investors rarely get first-day access, and how to avoid chasing IPO hype. Tools for this journey Investing → Portfolio → Private companies vs public companies A private company is owned by a small group — founders, employees, and private investors — and has no obligation to disclose its finances to the public. A public company sells shares on a stock exchange that anyone can buy, and in exchange it must regularly file detailed financial reports with the SEC , including quarterly and annual reports. Going from private to public changes more than who owns the stock. It exposes the company's financials, strategy, and executive pay to competitors, analysts, and short sellers, all watching every quarterly report. Some founders treat that scrutiny as the price of access to public capital; others see it as a reason to stay private as long as they can. How a company goes public: the IPO process A company goes public by hiring investment banks, called underwriters, to manage the offering, then filing a detailed registration statement with the SEC — searchable on the SEC's EDGAR system — that discloses its financials, risks, and business model. The SEC reviews the filing and can require changes before the offering proceeds. Once the filing clears review, the company and its underwriters go on a roadshow, pitching the stock to large institutional investors to gauge demand. That demand helps set the IPO price the night before trading begins. On the first trading day, the stock starts trading on the exchange, and its price can move sharply away from the IPO price within hours. The real benefits of going public Going public gives a company a large, one-time cash infusion it can use to pay down debt, fund growth, or acquire other companies. A public listing also creates a liquid stock that lets employees and early investors finally sell shares they've held for years, and it gives the company a public currency — its own stock — to use for future acquisitions. A public listing can also raise a company's profile with customers and partners, since a stock ticker carries a kind of credibility a private company doesn't have. For many founders and early employees, an IPO is the main way years of equity compensation finally turns into cash. Why an IPO can actually be a bad idea for the company Going public isn't automatically the right move, and plenty of successful companies choose to stay private for exactly that reason. The ongoing costs are real: compliance, quarterly reporting, investor relations staff, and far more exposure to shareholder lawsuits than a private company ever faces. Public markets also pressure management toward short-term results, since missing a single quarterly earnings estimate can hit the stock hard, even when the long-term strategy is sound. A company that needs years to execute a plan may find that pressure genuinely destructive, which is why some late-stage private companies raise plenty of cash from private investors and delay going public for as long as they can. How IPOs actually work for retail investors Retail investors — individuals buying through an ordinary brokerage account — almost never get shares at the IPO price on day one. The SEC's investor bulletin on IPOs notes that underwriters distribute most IPO shares to their institutional and high-net-worth clients first, so most retail investors can only buy once the stock starts trading on the open market, often at a price already well above the IPO price. A second risk shows up months later: the lockup period. Company insiders and early investors typically sign a lockup agreement , most commonly 180 days, that bars them from selling shares right after the IPO. When that lockup expires, a wave of insider selling can hit the stock all at once — the expiration date is disclosed in the prospectus, so retail investors can see it coming and plan around it instead of being surprised. The first-day 'pop' also isn't guaranteed to hold. A stock that jumps 40% on day one can just as easily give that gain back, or fall below its IPO price entirely, in the weeks and months that follow, once the initial demand from underpricing and hype fades. Once a company lists, you buy it like any other stock; SpaceX, which began trading on Nasdaq as SPCX on June 12, 2026, is a recent example, and our guide on how to buy SpaceX stock now that it's public walks through the order. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq as ANT on November 19, 2026; our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock covers the post-IPO price and lock-up details. Tips for investing in IPOs without chasing the hype Read the prospectus before you buy, not the headlines about the deal. The SEC recommends studying the actual offering document, since it discloses the company's finances, risks, and how shares are being allocated, in far more detail than any news story will. Watch for recency and hype bias: a stock dominating your social feed the week of its IPO is exactly the stock priced for maximum optimism, which leaves the least room for good news to push it higher. Waiting for the lockup expiration to pass, and for a full quarter or two of public reporting, gives you real financial data to evaluate instead of a roadshow pitch. Size any single IPO position small relative to your overall portfolio. A single new stock, with no trading history and a wave of insider selling still ahead of it, carries far more risk than an established company — our portfolio calculator can help you see how one volatile position affects your overall risk before you buy. Frequently asked questions What does IPO mean? IPO stands for initial public offering, the first time a private company sells shares to the public and begins trading on a stock exchange. Before the IPO, the company's shares are held by founders, employees, and private investors. Can regular investors buy shares at the IPO price? Rarely. Underwriters distribute most IPO shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients before trading opens, so most retail investors buy on the open market once trading begins, often at a price already above the IPO price. What is an IPO lockup period? A lockup period is a set window, most commonly 180 days, during which company insiders and early investors agree not to sell their shares after the IPO. When the lockup expires, a surge of insider selling can push the stock price down. Why do IPO stocks sometimes drop after their first day? A first-day 'pop' often reflects initial hype and intentional underpricing by underwriters, not the company's long-term value. As that early demand fades and the lockup expiration approaches, the stock can give back its early gains or fall below its IPO price. Why would a company avoid going public? Going public adds ongoing costs — compliance, quarterly reporting, investor relations, and shareholder lawsuit exposure — plus pressure to hit short-term earnings targets. Some companies with long-term strategies choose to stay private and raise cash from private investors instead. Is it risky to invest in a company's IPO? Yes, IPOs carry more risk than established public stocks because there's little public trading history, and a wave of insider selling is often still ahead at the lockup expiration. Reading the prospectus, sizing the position small, and waiting past the initial hype all help manage that risk. What is the difference between an IPO and a stock? An IPO is an event where a private company sells shares to the public for the first time, while a stock is the actual share of ownership you hold. Once that offering concludes, those same shares trade on the open market as ordinary public stock. The practical difference for buyers comes down to access and pricing. Underwriters set the IPO price the night before trading begins and distribute most of those initial shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients first. Most retail investors must wait until trading opens on the exchange, where they often pay a price already above that initial offering figure. mainEntity.name: What does IPO mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: IPO stands for initial public offering, the first time a private company sells shares to the public and begins trading on a stock exchange. Before the IPO, the company's shares are held by founders, employees, and private investors.

mainEntity.name: Can regular investors buy shares at the IPO price?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rarely. Underwriters distribute most IPO shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients before trading opens, so most retail investors buy on the open market once trading begins, often at a price already above the IPO price.

mainEntity.name: What is an IPO lockup period?

acceptedAnswer.text: A lockup period is a set window, most commonly 180 days, during which company insiders and early investors agree not to sell their shares after the IPO. When the lockup expires, a surge of insider selling can push the stock price down.

mainEntity.name: Why do IPO stocks sometimes drop after their first day?

acceptedAnswer.text: A first-day 'pop' often reflects initial hype and intentional underpricing by underwriters, not the company's long-term value. As that early demand fades and the lockup expiration approaches, the stock can give back its early gains or fall below its IPO price.

mainEntity.name: Why would a company avoid going public?

acceptedAnswer.text: Going public adds ongoing costs — compliance, quarterly reporting, investor relations, and shareholder lawsuit exposure — plus pressure to hit short-term earnings targets. Some companies with long-term strategies choose to stay private and raise cash from private investors instead.

mainEntity.name: Is it risky to invest in a company's IPO?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, IPOs carry more risk than established public stocks because there's little public trading history, and a wave of insider selling is often still ahead at the lockup expiration. Reading the prospectus, sizing the position small, and waiting past the initial hype all help manage that risk.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between an IPO and a stock?

acceptedAnswer.text: An IPO is an event where a private company sells shares to the public for the first time, while a stock is the actual share of ownership you hold. Once that offering concludes, those same shares trade on the open market as ordinary public stock. The practical difference for buyers comes down to access and pricing. Underwriters set the IPO price the night before trading begins and distribute most of those initial shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients first. Most retail investors must wait until trading opens on the exchange, where they often pay a price already above that initial offering figure.

Medicaid Work Requirements 2027: Will You Lose Coverage? By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated November 25, 2026 · How we review You will not automatically lose Medicaid coverage on January 1, 2027, if your state elects the federal hold-harmless option or if you qualify for a statutory exemption. Under federal guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), states adopting the transition relief may pause denials and terminations for community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. Beneficiaries must still complete scheduled renewals and report qualifying hours or exemption circumstances to keep their files in good standing. Who the Rule Covers and Who Is Exempt What a Hold-Harmless State Can and Cannot Do State Check Table What to Do Now Our Takeaway on the 2027 Work Requirement Will You Lose Medicaid on January 1? You will not automatically lose Medicaid on January 1, 2027, for missing the community engagement benchmark, but your immediate protection depends directly on whether your state chooses to pause disenrollments. Under section 71119 of Public Law 119-21, often called the Working Families Tax Cut legislation, the federal baseline requires states to implement community engagement rules no later than January 1, 2027. However, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ( CMS ) released State Medicaid Director Letter SMD# 26-006 on November 13, 2026, granting states an optional hold-harmless transition window. In a state that formally elects this hold-harmless period, the Medicaid agency can suspend all eligibility denials and disenrollments based on community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. This suspension applies to initial applications submitted and redetermination renewals initiated through that mid-year date. Even in participating states, administrators must still collect information and assess whether members meet the engagement rules. Enrollees must continue submitting paperwork, but coverage cannot be terminated strictly for failing the work requirement during this window. In states that do not adopt the hold-harmless policy, standard enforcement procedures begin immediately at the start of 2027. If an individual in an enforcement state fails to demonstrate required hours or an exemption, the state agency cannot terminate benefits without warning. Federal regulations under the CMS Interim Final Rule (IFR) require the agency to send a formal noncompliance notice. Beneficiaries then receive a window of 30 calendar days to submit proof of qualifying activities or claim an exemption before disenrollment takes effect. Who the Rule Covers and Who Is Exempt The federal community engagement mandate applies strictly to non-pregnant adults ages 19 through 64 who are enrolled in the Medicaid expansion adult group or certain section 1115 minimum essential coverage demonstrations across 43 states and the District of Columbia. United States territories are not subject to the mandate, and individuals entitled to or enrolled in Medicare are excluded from these requirements. To satisfy the standard, covered adults must log at least 80 hours per month of qualifying activities or earn wages equal to at least 80 times the federal minimum wage, which equals $580 per month in 2026. Qualifying activities can be combined to reach the 80-hour monthly threshold. Approved activities include work, community service, a work program, or half-time education, or a combination. When checking compliance, state agencies review past records: applicants must demonstrate compliance for at least one month prior to application, while existing enrollees are checked across one or more months between redetermination cycles as determined by individual state rules. Federal policy provides explicit statutory exemptions that protect vulnerable groups from disenrollment. According to official CMS documentation, you are exempt from the 80-hour monthly rule if you meet any of the following criteria: * You are pregnant or postpartum. * You are a parent or primary caretaker responsible for a child age 13 or younger, or you care for an individual with a recognized disability. * You are a former foster youth. * You are an American Indian or Alaska Native individual. * You are a totally disabled veteran. * You are deemed medically frail. * You are in substance use disorder treatment. * You are currently complying with existing work requirements under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). * You are currently incarcerated in a correctional facility. If you qualify for any exemption, you must notify your state agency to ensure your administrative record is coded appropriately. What a Hold-Harmless State Can and Cannot Do State Medicaid Director Letter SMD# 26-006 establishes clear boundaries regarding state authority during the transition. A state that elects the hold-harmless option receives federal protection against CMS enforcement actions if it chooses to halt adverse eligibility decisions. Under this mechanism, the state Medicaid program can suspend both application denials and mid-year disenrollments for individuals who do not show compliance with community engagement standards. States have the flexibility to implement this relief for the entire period through June 30, 2027, or choose a shorter calendar duration that suits their technical rollout schedules. Electing the hold-harmless policy does not allow a state to pause normal Medicaid verification standards. States are expressly required to build reporting mechanisms, gather activity documentation, and evaluate whether applicants qualify for exemptions. States intending to use the hold-harmless option starting January 1, 2027, were asked by CMS to submit notifications by December 11, 2026, through their formal community engagement mitigation plans. The hold-harmless period applies only to community engagement standards under section 1902(xx)(1) of the Social Security Act and 42 CFR 435.559. A state may not suspend denials or disenrollments for other eligibility factors, such as age or household income. As verified on November 23, 2026, by the Oregon Health Authority (OHA), Oregon is the one state this page verified from a primary source as having elected the hold-harmless period. Other states may also elect it, so check your own state Medicaid agency. OHA confirmed that no Oregon Health Plan member will face coverage denials or disenrollment for community engagement noncompliance through June 30, 2027. Oregon state officials noted that more than 600,000 members received informational notices in September 2026, and internal projections estimated that up to one-third of covered adults risked losing access purely due to reporting hurdles. Implementation also occurs alongside ongoing legal developments: on October 29, 2026, the federal district court in Massachusetts v. Oz partially vacated specific CMS regulatory limits regarding medical condition exemptions, which CMS formally acknowledged in footnote three of SMD# 26-006. State Check Table The table below shows what each situation means after January 1, 2027, according to CMS and the Oregon Health Authority. Situation What the state may do What you do Source Your state elected the hold harmless period and you cannot show 80 hours, $580 a month or an exemption May suspend denials and disenrollments for failing to show compliance, for applications received and renewals initiated through June 30, 2027 (or a shorter state period) Keep reporting and verifying; ask your state Medicaid agency how long its period lasts CMS SMD# 26-006 Your state did not elect it and you cannot show them Sends a noncompliance notice, then you have 30 calendar days to show compliance or an exemption Answer any notice within 30 calendar days with proof of hours, income or an exemption CMS fact sheet You meet an exemption Must assess whether you qualify for an exclusion or exception Report the exemption and keep records CMS fact sheet You are applying for Medicaid Checks the requirement at application, looking back at least one month; an electing state may suspend denials for applications received through June 30, 2027 Gather proof before you apply CMS fact sheet; SMD# 26-006 You live in Oregon Oregon opted in: no loss or denial of coverage for failing the rules through June 30, 2027 Still verify requirements or exemptions; you get more time at your next renewal Oregon Health Authority Ask your state Medicaid agency which row applies to you. What to Do Now Take these steps whether or not your state has adopted the hold harmless period. Ask your state Medicaid agency whether your state elected the hold harmless period and when it ends. Decide how you will document compliance before your next renewal. If you work, collect pay stubs, earnings statements or tax records showing at least $580 in gross monthly income or 80 logged hours. If you meet an exemption, gather your records now. Watch your mail for notices. In a state that has not delayed enforcement, a noncompliance notice gives you 30 calendar days to respond. If your income rises above Medicaid limits or you lose coverage, compare Marketplace plans. Our ACA vs Medicaid comparison explains the differences, and our free ACA subsidy calculator estimates premium tax credits and your out-of-pocket cost. Our Takeaway on the 2027 Work Requirement For most Medicaid expansion adults ages 19 through 64, the January 1, 2027 deadline poses immediate risk only if your state declined CMS hold-harmless relief and you cannot demonstrate 80 monthly activity hours, $580 in gross earnings, or an approved exemption category. In an opted-in state such as Oregon, the Medicaid agency cannot deny applications or disenroll enrollees for noncompliance before July 1, 2027, but your legal duty to report hours and complete redetermination forms remains active. This landscape would shift if CMS alters national transition guidelines, if additional states withdraw or submit mitigation plans, or if federal litigation in Massachusetts v. Oz expands court-ordered injunctions against enforcement. Frequently Asked Questions Does missing the work requirement cause immediate cancellation on January 1? No. In states participating in the CMS hold-harmless transition, disenrollment for community engagement noncompliance is paused through June 30, 2027. In non-participating states, federal rules require the agency to send a written noncompliance notice providing 30 calendar days to submit documentation or claim an exemption before terminating coverage. Can I combine part-time employment with school or volunteering? Yes. Federal guidelines let you combine qualifying activities, such as work, community service, a work program or half-time education, to reach the 80-hour monthly minimum. What earnings level satisfies the Medicaid community engagement requirement without tracking hours? Earning gross monthly wages equal to at least 80 times the federal minimum wage satisfies the requirement without logging separate hours. In 2026, earning at least $580 per month fulfills the standard. Does the hold-harmless delay protect me if my income exceeds Medicaid limits? No. The hold harmless period in CMS State Medicaid Director Letter SMD# 26-006 applies only to community engagement. States may not suspend denials or disenrollments for other eligibility factors, such as age or household income. How do I confirm whether my state opted into the hold-harmless extension? Check with your state Medicaid agency. Oregon is the one state this page verified from a primary source as having elected the hold harmless period through June 30, 2027, and other states may also elect it. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) raised the baseline conforming loan limit (CLL) by $22,650 from the 2026 level of $832,750, tracking a 2.72 percent rise in third-quarter average national home prices. In designated high-cost housing markets, the ceiling reaches $1,283,100, while special statutory provisions set higher baseline and ceiling levels in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Because the conforming limit caps the total amount borrowed rather than the property purchase price, your down payment determines exactly how expensive a home you can buy before leaving the conforming mortgage market. Tools for this journey Down Payment Calculator → Home Affordability Calculator → Types of Mortgage Loans → The 2027 Conforming Loan Limit The 2027 baseline conforming loan limit for one-unit properties is $855,400 across the majority of United States counties. This represents an increase of $22,650 over the 2026 baseline limit of $832,750. Under federal statutory formulas, the baseline limit adjusts annually based on changes in the national average home price between the third quarter of the previous year and the third quarter of the current year. Between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, average home prices increased by 2.72 percent, and FHFA applied that identical 2.72 percent rate of increase to the baseline loan threshold. In high-cost areas where local median home values exceed the national baseline, federal law establishes a local ceiling calculated at 150 percent of the baseline conforming limit. For one-unit properties in these high-cost counties, the 2027 ceiling is $1,283,100. Specific statutory exceptions apply to Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In those four designated regions, the local baseline limit is set at $1,283,100 and the maximum high-cost ceiling reaches $1,924,650 for a single-family one-unit residence. Conforming loan limits define the maximum dollar size of a mortgage that government-sponsored enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can acquire. These limits apply specifically to the total principal balance of the mortgage note, not to the contract purchase price of the real estate. When a buyer submits a down payment, the loan amount represents only the remaining unpaid balance. A homebuyer purchasing a property priced above $855,400 can still obtain a conforming loan as long as their cash down payment reduces the total borrowed principal to $855,400 or less. Purchase Price Before a Loan Becomes Jumbo In our internal calculation, we modeled the relationship between down payment percentages and maximum purchase prices to show how much home you can buy before crossing into jumbo financing. Using the mathematical formula of purchase price equal to loan limit divided by one minus the down payment share, we calculated the maximum transaction value supported by conforming loans at baseline and high-cost limits. The table below outlines these thresholds for one-unit properties across standard down payment levels of 3 percent, 5 percent, 10 percent, 15 percent, and 20 percent. Baseline counties, loan at the $855,400 limit: Down payment Down payment in dollars Highest purchase price a conforming loan can finance 3% $26,456 $881,856 5% $45,021 $900,421 10% $95,044 $950,444 15% $150,953 $1,006,353 20% $213,850 $1,069,250 High-cost counties, loan at the $1,283,100 ceiling: Down payment Down payment in dollars Highest purchase price a conforming loan can finance 3% $39,684 $1,322,784 5% $67,532 $1,350,632 10% $142,567 $1,425,667 15% $226,429 $1,509,529 20% $320,775 $1,603,875 The formula is purchase price = loan limit / (1 - down payment share). To test specific down payment figures and equity amounts for your budget, use our down payment calculator . Understanding Down Payment Math and Equity Impact Every extra dollar added to a down payment lowers the amount you borrow by one dollar. If your loan lands slightly above the limit, a larger down payment can bring it back under. The table assumes closing costs and prepaid items are paid in cash rather than added to the loan. If fees or financed insurance premiums are added to the loan principal, the purchase price a conforming loan supports is lower. A lender may also set its own thresholds. Find Your County Limit While $855,400 is the nationwide baseline, the conforming loan limit is higher than baseline in all but 24 counties or county equivalents across the United States. In the remaining counties where local median home values exceed baseline calculations, the limit scales upward between $855,400 and the high-cost ceiling of $1,283,100. Homebuyers must check the specific limit assigned to the county where the subject property is located rather than relying on national figures alone. To identify your local lending threshold, consult the official county datasets provided on the FHFA conforming loan limit page . The agency publishes comprehensive downloadable county lists, interactive mapping resources, a technical methodology addendum, and detailed administrative guidelines. These documents list every county and county equivalent by state. In high-cost areas, county limits reach the maximum ceiling of $1,283,100. Many suburban or intermediate housing markets feature custom limits established between the baseline and the ceiling. The baseline figures modeled in our table serve as a legal floor. For any county with an elevated limit, the maximum purchase price supported by a conforming loan will be higher than the baseline figures at every down payment level. Does Waiting until January Help? Waiting until January 2027 to finalize a mortgage transaction only benefits borrowers borrowing within a specific dollar window. Because the baseline limit increases from $832,750 in 2026 to $855,400 in 2027, the potential advantage applies exclusively to loan amounts between $832,750 and $855,400 in baseline counties. If your anticipated loan balance is below $832,750, the loan already meets conforming standards under 2026 rules. If your loan balance exceeds $855,400, the mortgage remains non-conforming regardless of the annual calendar change unless your county features a higher localized limit. Even for loans falling inside that $22,650 band, waiting until January does not guarantee conforming treatment without direct lender confirmation. FHFA states in its official documentation that conforming loan limits apply to mortgages acquired by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in the 2027 calendar year. The agency's public data pages tie the limits to the calendar year in which the loan is acquired and do not state a specific loan delivery rule or origination date rule. Mortgage lenders establish their own pipeline policies regarding when they begin applying upcoming loan limits to newly originated applications. You must ask your lender directly which annual limit applies to your specific closing date. What Changes If You Go Jumbo A loan above the conforming limit in your county is a jumbo loan. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac cannot acquire it under the 2027 limit, so each lender sets its own underwriting rules and terms for it. Ask each lender for its jumbo requirements and rates before you commit. To compare jumbo financing with conventional, government-insured and other options, read our breakdown of types of mortgage loans . Our Takeaway If your total borrowed mortgage balance is $855,400 or less, your loan qualifies as conforming across all United States counties in 2027. Mixed-status families who have not already submitted verification will keep prorated rent help only temporarily while their documentation is pending, with a strict 90-day deadline from the effective date to submit proof. A federal lawsuit led by New York and 20 other states plus the District of Columbia, joined by Pennsylvania's governor, is currently challenging the rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Because no court has issued an injunction or vacatur, the federal rule remains scheduled to take effect as written. Tools for this journey Rent Budget Planning Guide → On This Page What Changes on December 14 Who Is Affected and Which Programs Are Covered Timeline Table Timeline and Deadlines for Mixed-Status Families The Multistate Lawsuit Challenging the Rule What Tenants and Assisted Families Should Do Now Our Takeaway on HUD Verification Requirements What Changes on December 14 The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) published its final rule in the Federal Register on November 12, 2026, under document number FR 2026-23003 , titled Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status (91 FR 72978). This regulation carries an official effective date of December 14, 2026. The most consequential change in the regulation revises HUD's Section 214 rules by requiring verification of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status for every individual applicant and recipient of assistance under covered programs, regardless of how old the family member is. Under regulations that existed prior to this final rule, mixed-status families were permitted to live together in subsidized housing while receiving prorated assistance. In those arrangements, a household received a partial rent subsidy calculated strictly for the members who had verified citizenship or eligible immigration status, while members without eligible status received no direct subsidy. Under those prior standards, an individual family member could elect not to contend eligible status. Choosing that option meant the individual did not have to submit immigration documents, and the family simply accepted a smaller, prorated subsidy that reflected only the eligible members. The final rule published on November 12 completely eliminates that option. Going forward, every person living in an assisted unit must have their status affirmatively verified. Prorated assistance is no longer an ongoing arrangement that a family can maintain indefinitely. Instead, the final rule redefines prorated assistance as a temporary status that only applies while the verification of all household members is actively pending, where permitted by statute. If any member of the household cannot or does not establish eligible status, the family can no longer rely on long-term proration to maintain subsidized tenancy under covered housing programs. Who Is Affected and Which Programs Are Covered The reach of the regulation is defined by the underlying statutory authorities governing federal housing subsidies. According to HUD's official guidance and the Federal Register preamble, the final rule applies specifically to Section 214 covered programs. The covered programs include Section 236 of the National Housing Act, specifically for tenants paying below-market rent. They also include programs authorized under the United States Housing Act of 1937: Public Housing, the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program, Project-based Section 8 rental assistance, and low-income units supported by Housing Development Grants. In contrast, HUD explicitly identifies several multifamily programs that are not covered by this Section 214 final rule. The excluded categories are Section 202 and Section 811 Project Rental Assistance Contracts (202/811 PRAC), Section 811 Project Rental Assistance (811 PRA), Senior Preservation Rental Assistance Contracts (SPRAC), and Section 202/162 Project Assistance Contracts (202/162 PAC). Households residing in units subsidized strictly under these excluded programs are not subject to the new verification mandate or the removal of the election not to contend eligible status. According to HUD estimates cited in the New York Attorney General's Nov 23, 2026 release , approximately 20,000 mixed-status families nationwide could lose their rental assistance under the new mandate. Those households encompass roughly 78,100 individual residents. Notably, the same estimates indicate that about 55,000 of the individuals who stand to lose assistance are fully eligible residents themselves, mostly children. Timeline Table The table below lists the dates that matter, in order. Date or trigger What happens Source Nov 12, 2026 HUD publishes the final rule (91 FR 72978) Federal Register Nov 23, 2026 New York and 20 other states plus the District of Columbia, joined by Pennsylvania's governor, file suit in the District of Massachusetts New York Attorney General Dec 14, 2026 Rule takes effect Federal Register Within 30 days after Dec 14 Housing authority or owner must send the Section 214 notice to tenants who have not submitted evidence Federal Register Within 90 days of Dec 14 (about Mar 14, 2027) Mixed-status families must submit evidence Federal Register Next annual or interim reexamination All other tenants must submit evidence Federal Register On certification Written extension of up to 60 days in total Federal Register This second table shows which programs the rule covers. Program Covered by the rule Source Public Housing Yes Federal Register; HUD Housing Choice Vouchers Yes HUD Project-based Section 8 Yes HUD Section 236 (tenants paying below-market rent only) Yes Federal Register Housing Development Grant programs (low-income units only) Yes Federal Register 202/811 PRAC, 811 PRA, SPRAC, 202/162 PAC No HUD Timeline and Deadlines for Mixed-Status Families The regulation creates two separate compliance tracks depending on whether a household is currently classified as a mixed-status family. The shortest timeline applies directly to mixed-status families who are already receiving assistance but have members who have not submitted verification evidence. For tenants in mixed families who have not submitted proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status as of December 14, 2026, the final rule requires that all required documentation be submitted within 90 days of December 14, 2026. That 90-day window sets the initial deadline at approximately March 14, 2027. For all other existing tenants in covered programs who have not previously submitted verification evidence, the timeline is longer. Those non-mixed households must submit proof at their next regular annual or interim reexamination of income and household composition scheduled after December 14, 2026. For applicants seeking admission to covered programs, verification documents must be submitted no later than the date when the housing provider examines other eligibility criteria. Housing providers and responsible entities have specific legal obligations during this rollout. Housing authorities and private property owners must deliver an official Section 214 notification to every tenant who has not yet submitted evidence no later than 30 days after the December 14 effective date. However, HUD specifically declined to tie the running of the 90-day compliance window to the date an individual tenant receives that letter. The 90-day clock runs strictly from the effective date of December 14, 2026. A tenant who cannot produce the necessary documents before the deadline may qualify for an extension. Under Section 5.508(g) of the rule, a housing authority or owner must grant an extension if the family submits the required declaration and consent forms certifying eligible status, certifies that the underlying documents are temporarily unavailable or more time is needed, and shows that prompt, diligent efforts will be made to obtain the evidence. Any extension granted under this provision must be issued in writing, cannot exceed 60 days in total, and cannot run concurrently with other submission timelines. The Multistate Lawsuit Challenging the Rule On November 23, 2026, a major legal challenge was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts seeking to invalidate HUD's final rule. The lawsuit is led by New York Attorney General Letitia James and represents a coalition of 22 attorneys general. The plaintiffs include New York and 20 other states plus the District of Columbia, joined by Pennsylvania's governor. The specific plaintiff states identified in the action are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, alongside New York. The complaint asserts that HUD exceeded its statutory authority under the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980. The states argue that Congress explicitly codified the ability of mixed-status families to receive prorated housing assistance through legislation enacted in 1997, and that HUD lacks the administrative authority to overwrite that statutory compromise by regulation. Furthermore, the coalition argues that HUD violates the Administrative Procedure Act. The lawsuit asks the federal court to issue a declaration, vacatur, and an injunction for plaintiff states. However, tenants and advocates must recognize that as of November 25, 2026, no court order, temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or vacatur has been granted. The filing of a lawsuit does not pause a federal regulation. Unless and until a federal judge signs an order blocking the rule, housing providers remain legally bound to implement the December 14, 2026 requirements. What Tenants and Assisted Families Should Do Now Do not leave your home or give up your voucher because of rumors. The rule sets notice periods and extensions, and a pending lawsuit does not stop it on its own. Contact your housing authority or property owner to confirm which program funds your unit and which family members have already submitted documents. Gather identity and status documents for every household member. Ask about an extension. A housing provider must grant one of up to 60 days in total if you certify that eligible status exists and that the evidence is temporarily unavailable, and you show diligent efforts to get it. Contact local legal aid or a tenant advocacy group about your household's records and the lawsuit. If a subsidy change could affect your budget, plan with our guide on how much to spend on rent . Our Takeaway on HUD Verification Requirements If your household resides in Public Housing, uses a Housing Choice Voucher, or lives in Project-based Section 8 housing, you should treat the December 14, 2026 effective date as an active deadline. Begin assembling proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status for every person listed on your lease immediately. Mixed-status families should not wait for their annual renewal date, because the regulation imposes a strict 90-day submission deadline measured directly from December 14, 2026, which expires on approximately March 14, 2027. This recommendation is based on the published regulatory text in Federal Register document 2026-23003 and the current procedural status of the federal docket. Our guidance would change if the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts or another federal court enters an order staying the effective date or granting a preliminary injunction, or if HUD formally issues an administrative stay or revised implementation timeline. Until an official court order or housing authority notice confirms a delay, tenants must assume the verification deadlines remain fully operative. Frequently Asked Questions What happens if a family cannot provide documents before the 90-day deadline? If a mixed-status family cannot provide documentation within the 90-day window following December 14, 2026, the household can request a formal extension. Under Section 5.508(g) of the final rule, housing providers must grant an extension of up to 60 days if the family submits forms certifying that unverified members hold eligible status and explains in writing that documents are temporarily unavailable despite diligent efforts. If a family fails to submit documentation after the deadline and any granted extension, consequences follow under paragraph (h) of the rule. Does the multistate lawsuit stop the rule from taking effect on December 14? No. The filing of a federal complaint does not pause or block a federal regulation. A coalition of 22 attorneys general, led by New York and joined by Pennsylvania's governor, filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on November 23, 2026, seeking an injunction and vacatur. However, as of November 25, 2026, no court order or injunction has been issued. The rule remains scheduled to take effect on December 14, 2026, unless a judge issues a stay before that date. Can mixed-status families still elect not to contend eligible status? No. Under prior HUD regulations, family members could elect not to contend eligible immigration status, which allowed the household to receive prorated assistance without submitting immigration papers for those individuals. The final rule published on November 12, 2026, officially eliminates the election not to contend eligible status. Every member of an assisted household under covered programs must now have their eligible status verified. Are Section 202 and Section 811 housing programs affected by the rule? HUD's page lists the 202/811 PRAC, 811 PRA, SPRAC and 202/162 PAC programs as not covered. Public Housing, Housing Choice Vouchers and Project-based Section 8 are covered. Ask your housing authority or owner which program funds your unit. How will tenants be notified about the new verification requirements? The final rule requires responsible entities, such as local public housing authorities or private property owners participating in covered programs, to issue an official Section 214 notice to each tenant who has not yet submitted proof of citizenship or eligible status. This notice must be sent no later than 30 days after the December 14, 2026 effective date. However, the 90-day compliance period for mixed-status families runs from December 14, 2026, rather than the date the notice is received. The IRS lists this as a premium tax credit condition: the person enrolled in Marketplace coverage must not be eligible for coverage through a government program such as Medicaid or CHIP. HealthCare.gov puts it plainly: "If you qualify for Medicaid, you aren't eligible for savings on a Marketplace plan." Declining Medicaid does not restore the savings. A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan generally pays full price for the premium and for covered services. A child may also lose CHIP eligibility if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is one exception. Some limited types of Medicaid pay only for family planning, treatment of an emergency medical condition, or tuberculosis services. When a Medicaid program does not count as minimum essential coverage, the person may be eligible for premium tax credits and other Marketplace savings if they qualify based on income and other criteria. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid minimum essential coverage lookup shows, by state, whether a given Medicaid program counts and what action to take. People with limited Medicaid can also fill out a Marketplace application to find out whether they qualify for full-benefit Medicaid or a Marketplace plan with savings. Medicaid status is one of several federal tests. The IRS lists these premium tax credit requirements: Household income generally from 100 percent to 400 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL) for the family size. A filing status other than married filing separately, apart from a special rule for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. Not being claimable as a dependent by another person. No access to affordable employer coverage that provides minimum value for the person enrolled. Payment of the share of premiums not covered by advance credit payments. A timing rule applies when status changes mid-year. The Marketplace may find someone ineligible for Medicaid at enrollment and approve advance credit payments. In that case, the IRS generally treats the person as ineligible for Medicaid for the rest of the plan year, even if Medicaid later approves coverage. The IRS still tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. HealthCare.gov says each state's coverage options consider income, household size, family status such as pregnancy or caring for young children, disability, age and other factors. Some states expanded Medicaid to cover adults below a certain income level, and others did not. HealthCare.gov advises applying for Medicaid even when income looks too high. HealthCare.gov's federal poverty level table lists 2026 amounts of $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four, with higher amounts in Alaska and Hawaii. Income below 100 percent probably will not qualify for Marketplace savings but may qualify for Medicaid. Marketplace savings use expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Medicaid income rules vary by state and eligibility category. HealthCare.gov's income guide defines MAGI as adjusted gross income plus untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits and tax-exempt interest, without Supplemental Security Income. Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year rather than last year's income. Self-employed applicants count the income they expect to make from the business after expenses. For income that is hard to predict, HealthCare.gov says to report current income, review the yearly estimate it shows, and update the application as changes happen. Members of one household can end up in different programs. HealthCare.gov notes that children may qualify for CHIP even when a parent does not qualify for Medicaid. On a Marketplace application, if anyone in the household looks eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, the Marketplace securely sends that information to the state agency, which then contacts the household about enrollment. Use two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 monthly plan premium. Assume every other eligibility condition is met, including that no one is eligible for Medicaid. Income is 138.63% of FPL, the applicable percentage is about 3.58%, and the monthly contribution is $89.61. The benchmark minus that contribution is far more than the $100 plan premium. The credit cannot exceed the $100 plan premium, so the credit is $100 and the net premium is $0. Read together, the two cases show how each input works. Income sets the contribution. Government coverage: a person eligible for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) , Medicare, or another government program that counts as qualifying health coverage cannot get the credit for that person's Marketplace coverage. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count is an exception. Employer offers: an offer for 2027 plan years is generally affordable if the employee's self-only premium share is no more than 10.22% of household income. Filing rules: married couples who file separately generally cannot claim the credit, with an exception for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. If the advance payments were larger than the final credit, the IRS sets no repayment cap for tax years after 2025. The full difference reduces your refund or raises your balance due, and if the final credit is larger, the difference goes to you. An affordable employer offer, qualifying government coverage, or changed law or plan prices can reverse it. The ACA premium tax credit is based on expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) compared with the federal poverty level for your household size, plus the benchmark Silver premium for your coverage family. The income sets your contribution, the benchmark minus that contribution sets the credit, and the premium of the plan you enroll in caps it. How to qualify for ACA subsidy? You must meet every IRS eligibility condition. Income alone cannot establish eligibility. Household income must fall in the allowed range. Married filing separately generally prevents the credit, with a limited abuse or abandonment exception. No one else can claim you as a dependent. The covered person must enroll in a non-catastrophic Marketplace plan and lack affordable employer coverage. Eligibility for qualifying government coverage, such as most Medicaid or Medicare, prevents the credit. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as qualifying coverage is an exception. The covered person must pay the share of premiums the credit does not cover. What is the maximum ACA subsidy? The ACA subsidy can be as large as the full premium of the plan you enroll in, because the IRS caps the credit at enrollment premiums. By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated October 26, 2026 · How we review This home affordability calculator uses your income, debts, down payment, and mortgage rate to estimate how much house you can afford. Enter your numbers above to see your target home price and monthly payment. Lenders compare your income with your debts to determine how much you can borrow. Knowing what you can afford before you start shopping helps keep your search realistic and your budget safe. $287,000 home you can afford $2,100 monthly budget $247,285 loan amount Share Interactive — edit any field How it's calculated The calculator above applies the 28/36 rule, a common guideline lenders use to gauge affordability. Under this rule, your monthly housing payment should stay at or below 28% of your gross monthly income, and your total debt payments should stay at or below 36%. Your gross income is what you earn before taxes. The lower of these two limits sets your real budget. The housing payment here means PITI, not just principal and interest. PITI stands for principal, interest, property taxes, and insurance. If your down payment is under 20%, lenders usually add private mortgage insurance (PMI), which raises the payment. Try our down payment calculator and closing cost calculator to plan the cash you'll need up front. One underwriting trap that stops otherwise-qualified buyers: unaddressed IRS back taxes. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac , and FHA (Handbook 4000.1) will not underwrite while there's IRS debt outstanding unless you're on a formal long-term installment agreement AND have made at least 3 monthly payments on time. A recorded Notice of Federal Tax Lien blocks approval entirely until it's released, discharged, or subordinated to the new mortgage. If back taxes are in the picture, the back taxes impact calculator shows exactly what stops the loan and how to clear each block. If your price range runs near the loan-size line for conventional loans, read about the 2027 conforming loan limit . Once you have a price range, the home buying checklist lays out what to do and check at each stage of the purchase. A worked example Say you earn $90,000 a year, or $7,500 in gross monthly income. You pay $400 a month toward existing debt, have $40,000 for a down payment, and face a 6.5% rate on a 30-year loan. Under the 28% housing limit, your maximum monthly payment is $2,100. That is the binding limit here, so it sets your budget. With property tax near 1.1% and insurance around $1,800 a year, you can afford a home priced at about $287,000, with a loan of roughly $247,285. The $2,100 payment breaks down to about $1,563 in principal and interest, $263 in property tax, $150 in insurance, and $124 in PMI, since the down payment is under 20%. Common mistakes to avoid Budgeting for only principal and interest. Property taxes, insurance, and PMI are part of every payment and can add hundreds of dollars a month. If you are buying in Minnesota, see why a Minnesota proposed tax can change your budget . Ignoring existing debt. A car loan or student loan payment shrinks your housing budget close to dollar for dollar under the 36% limit. Treating the lender's maximum as your target. Lenders may approve a debt-to-income ratio well above 36%, but a higher ratio leaves less room for emergencies. Using take-home pay instead of gross income. The 28/36 rule is based on income before taxes, so using net pay distorts the result. Forgetting closing costs and a cash cushion. Stretching your down payment to the limit can leave you short on move-in day and beyond. Frequently asked questions How does a home affordability calculator decide how much house I can afford? LTV is the figure lenders watch most. A 20% down payment means an 80% LTV, which avoids PMI on a conventional loan. Anything under 20% down pushes your LTV above 80% and usually adds PMI. Once you have a price in mind, see how much you can borrow with the home affordability calculator , and budget the rest with the closing cost calculator . Your down payment also changes the loan size, and loans above the conforming loan limit for 2027 are jumbo loans. A worked example Say you are buying a $400,000 home and put 10% down. Your down payment is $40,000, leaving a loan amount of $360,000. That puts your loan-to-value ratio at 90%. Because that is under 20% down, PMI is likely. If you could put down $40,000 more, your total down payment would reach $80,000, or 20%. That larger down payment would avoid PMI and lower both your loan and your lifetime interest. Common mistakes to avoid Assuming you must put 20% down. Conventional loans go as low as 3%, and FHA loans start at 3.5%. You can buy with far less. Forgetting that under 20% down usually means PMI. This extra cost is added to your monthly payment until you reach 20% equity. Budgeting only for the down payment. Closing costs are separate and due at the same time. Estimate them with the closing cost calculator. Treating PMI as permanent. You can request cancellation at 80% LTV, and it auto-terminates at 78% LTV under federal law. Draining all your savings into the down payment. Leave a cushion for moving, repairs, and emergencies after closing. Frequently asked questions How much down payment do I need? It depends on your loan type. Conventional loans can require as little as 3% down, and FHA loans require at least 3.5%. Use the down payment calculator above to turn a percent into a dollar amount for your home price. A 20% down payment is the threshold that avoids PMI on a conventional loan, but it is not required to buy. Does a down payment under 20% mean I pay PMI? Usually, yes. On a conventional loan, a down payment under 20% means your loan-to-value is above 80%, so lenders typically require private mortgage insurance (PMI). PMI protects the lender, not you. Every mortgage also pairs that loan type with a loan term, such as 15 or 30 years, and a rate type, fixed or adjustable. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) frames every home loan this way. Sometimes only one loan type fits your situation. If several fit, the CFPB suggests trying scenarios and asking lenders for several quotes to see which type offers the best deal overall. Tools for this journey Mortgage calculator → Mortgage affordability → FHA loan calculator → VA loan calculator → The Main Types of Mortgage Loans at a Glance Conventional loans make up the majority of mortgages, and the conforming version is the most common loan type. Government and housing agency programs serve specific borrowers, and which type costs least depends on your credit, your down payment and the programs you are eligible for. Loan type Who it is for What to know Conventional (conforming) The majority of loans. Conforming is the most common loan type. The government sets the maximum loan amount, and Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac set the other rules. Mortgage insurance is typically required with less than 20 percent down. Jumbo (non-conforming) Borrowers who need more than the conforming jumbo limit in their county Rules vary by lender. Borrowers usually need good credit and a high down payment. Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Borrowers with lower credit scores or a small down payment Down payments as low as 3.5 percent. Mortgage insurance is required on every FHA loan, and the maximum loan amount varies by county. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Veterans, service members and surviving spouses A Certificate of Eligibility shows the lender you qualify. Nearly 90 percent of VA-backed loans are made with no down payment. U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Low- to middle-income borrowers in rural areas Check eligibility with USDA before applying. State or local housing agency programs Low- to middle-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers or public service employees Offered by state or local housing agencies. Special Purpose Credit Programs are private-lender loans to low- to middle-income borrowers, generally in targeted communities. Three Choices Every Mortgage Combines Every mortgage combines three separate choices: a loan type, a loan term and an interest rate type. Picking a conventional loan does not settle the term or the rate. You still choose those on their own, and each one changes a different part of the deal. Choice Common options What it changes Loan type Conventional, FHA, VA, USDA, special programs Your down payment, your total cost including interest and mortgage insurance, and how much you can borrow Loan term 15 years or 30 years Your monthly payment, your interest rate and your total cost Rate type Fixed or adjustable Whether your principal and interest payment can change over the life of the loan The loan type also affects the house price range you can consider. A 30-year FHA loan and a 15-year FHA loan share a loan type but carry different monthly payments and different total costs. Conforming, Jumbo and Other Conventional Loans A conventional loan is any mortgage that is not part of a specific government program. Conventional loans typically cost less than FHA loans but can be more difficult to get. They split into two main categories, conforming and non-conforming. Conforming loans are the most common loan type. The government sets their maximum loan amounts, and Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, which back conforming loans, set the other rules. By law, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can only buy single-family mortgages below a ceiling called the conforming loan limit. Look up your county's figure on the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) conforming loan limit page before you set a price range. For the 2027 figures and what each down payment buys, see our guide to the 2027 conforming loan limit . The 2026 limits were set using the formula in the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, and they are higher in some high-cost areas. In certain counties, a conforming jumbo loan covers amounts above the standard limit, with a maximum that varies by county. Jumbo loans above the conforming jumbo limit in your county are non-conforming. Rules vary by lender, but borrowers usually need good credit and a high down payment. Non-conforming loans are less standardized, so eligibility, pricing and features can vary widely, and the CFPB calls shopping around particularly important for them. A third group, other non-conforming loans, covers loans of any size that fit no other category. Some are aimed at borrowers with poor credit and tend to carry high rates. They may also include minimal income documentation, interest-only payments or a balance that is allowed to increase. Many of the loans that got people in trouble during the financial crisis fell in this group. If you are offered one, consult several lenders and ask whether you could qualify for a conforming or FHA loan instead. If a lender pitches a portfolio loan, our portfolio loan explainer walks through how it works. On a conventional loan, a down payment under 20 percent typically means paying for mortgage insurance. Our FHA vs conventional loan comparison is the next read for buyers with a smaller down payment. Government-Backed Loans from FHA, VA and USDA Government-backed loans serve three groups: borrowers with lower credit scores or small down payments (FHA), veterans and service members (VA), and low- to middle-income rural borrowers (USDA). FHA loans come from private lenders and are regulated and insured by the Federal Housing Administration, a government agency that does not lend the money itself. They allow down payments as low as 3.5 percent and lower credit scores than most conventional loans. Mortgage insurance is required on every FHA loan, and the maximum loan amount varies by county. Whether FHA or conventional costs less depends on your profile. For borrowers with good credit and a 10 to 15 percent down payment, FHA loans tend to cost more than conventional loans. For borrowers with lower credit scores or smaller down payments, FHA can often be the cheapest option. The CFPB says there are no hard-and-fast rules and a lot depends on the current market, so ask lenders to quote both. The FHA loan calculator lets you test different down payments before you request quotes. VA home loans help Veterans, service members and their survivors buy, build, improve or refinance a home. VA offers a VA direct loan and 3 VA-backed loans, and nearly 90 percent of VA-backed loans are made with no down payment. A Certificate of Eligibility (COE), based on your service history and duty status, shows a lender that you qualify. A VA loan may offer better terms than a traditional loan from a private bank, mortgage company or credit union. You still need the required credit and income for the amount you borrow. Run your numbers in the VA loan calculator , then read our VA loan vs conventional loan comparison and FHA loan vs VA loan comparison . USDA loans are for low- to middle-income borrowers in rural areas. For how the two programs differ, see our USDA loan vs FHA loan comparison . Fixed-Rate vs Adjustable-Rate Mortgages A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate and the same monthly principal and interest payment. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) has a rate that can rise or fall after an initial period. Most borrowers choose fixed-rate mortgages. On a fixed-rate loan, your total monthly payment can still change if property taxes, homeowner's insurance or mortgage insurance change. An ARM starts with a lower interest rate. Most ARMs have two periods: an introductory period with a fixed rate, then a second period where the rate adjusts regularly. Part of the rate is tied to an index, and the rate you pay is the index plus a set margin, subject to any caps. After the fixed period ends, the monthly principal and interest payment can go up or down. It could go up a lot, even double. Some ARMs include rate caps that limit how much the rate can adjust. An ARM could cost less in the short term, for example if you plan to move within the initial fixed period. If you stay longer than expected, you could pay a lot more. The CFPB warns against assuming you can sell or refinance before the rate changes, because your property's value could drop or your finances could change. Before taking an ARM, get answers to five questions from the lender: How high or low can the rate and payment go with each adjustment? How often does the rate adjust? How soon could the payment go up? Is there a cap on how high the rate can go? Could you still afford the loan at the maximum rate and payment? To weigh the two rate types on cost and risk, read our fixed vs ARM mortgage comparison . Loan Term and the 15-Year vs 30-Year Tradeoff A shorter loan term means higher monthly payments, a typically lower interest rate and a lower total cost. A longer term reverses each of those: lower monthly payments, a typically higher rate and a higher total cost. The CFPB says the rate on a shorter term is usually lower, by as much as a full percentage point. How much lower depends on the terms and rates involved. Rates vary among lenders, especially for shorter terms, so ask each lender to quote both lengths. Our 15-year vs 30-year mortgage comparison covers the two terms, and the 40-year mortgage guide covers a longer term. Loan Features to Question Before You Sign The CFPB flags four loan features to be careful with: a prepayment penalty, a balloon payment, negative amortization and interest-only payments. If a loan offer includes one, ask the loan officer why. Then ask for a second Loan Estimate for the same loan without that feature, so you can see what the feature costs you. Generally, a lender must document and verify your income, employment, assets, debts and credit history to decide whether you can repay. A loan that does this and meets certain criteria may be called a qualified mortgage . Nonqualified mortgages can be riskier or more expensive. They are sometimes marketed to self-employed borrowers or borrowers without Social Security numbers. If you are offered one, compare Loan Estimates from several lenders. How to Compare Types of Mortgage Loans Compare types of mortgage loans by getting official Loan Estimates from several lenders for each type that fits you, then comparing the total cost. The CFPB says never make a final decision about a loan before you have Loan Estimates in hand. Start by narrowing the list on eligibility. A Certificate of Eligibility shows a VA lender that you qualify, and USDA loans are for low- to middle-income rural borrowers. Conforming loans stop at your county's limit, and anything above it is a jumbo loan. Your down payment and credit shape the rest. FHA can often be cheapest with a lower credit score or a small down payment. Conventional tends to cost less with good credit and a 10 to 15 percent down payment. Set a price range with the mortgage affordability calculator , then test terms and rates in the mortgage calculator . Our best mortgage lenders roundup helps you build a shortlist, and our list of questions to ask a mortgage lender covers what to raise on each call. If this is your first purchase, the first-time home buyer guide walks through the steps around the loan. Frequently asked questions What is the most common mortgage type? Conforming conventional loans are the most common type. Conventional loans make up the majority of mortgages, and conforming loans follow maximum loan amounts set by the government plus other rules set by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. On rate type, most borrowers choose a fixed-rate mortgage. What are the five major types of mortgages? The CFPB sorts mortgages into three categories: conventional, government and special programs. Within them, the main loan types are conforming, jumbo, FHA, VA, USDA and state or local housing agency programs. Each type can then pair with a loan term and a fixed or adjustable rate. What is a jumbo mortgage loan? A jumbo mortgage is a loan above the conforming loan limit, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes each year and which varies by county. Some counties allow conforming jumbo loans above the standard limit. Loans above that county figure are non-conforming jumbo loans. What is a hybrid ARM mortgage? A hybrid ARM is an adjustable-rate mortgage that starts with a fixed rate for an introductory period, then adjusts regularly after that. Once adjustments begin, the rate follows an index plus a set margin, subject to any caps, so the monthly payment can rise or fall. The CFPB warns against assuming you can sell or refinance before the rate changes. What are the risks of a mortgage? Risks the CFPB names include rising ARM payments and risky loan features. An ARM payment can go up a lot after the fixed period, even double. Prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization and interest-only payments all call for caution, and nonqualified mortgages can be riskier or more expensive. Ask for a Loan Estimate without the feature to compare. What is the best type of home mortgage loan? No single type is best for every buyer. The right fit depends on your down payment, your credit, which programs you are eligible for, and how long you plan to stay in the home.
